title: Foreign Trade
tagline: Import, export and entrepot trade, the balance of trade, and the documents that carry a consignment across a border. Unit weight: 10 marks.

overview.intro: Selling abroad changes almost every risk a trader carries. The buyer may be unreachable, the goods may be held at a port for weeks, the currency may move against the contract, and the law of two countries may apply at once. Trade survives these risks because it runs on documents: a defined set of instruments that a bank, a customs authority and a shipping line will each accept as proof of the same transaction. This unit covers the forms of foreign trade and its importance, the balance of trade and balance of payments, and the principal documents used in carrying out foreign trade.

learningOutcomes: Define foreign trade and its three forms.
Explain the importance of foreign trade to an economy.
Distinguish balance of trade from balance of payments.
List and state the purpose of the principal export and import documents.
Explain the role of a letter of credit in an overseas transaction.

learn.title: Meaning, forms and importance of foreign trade

blocks.text: Foreign trade is the trade between residents of different countries, and it takes three forms. Import trade brings goods into the country. Export trade sends goods out of it. Entrepot trade brings goods in, often processes or repackages them, and sends them on to a third country, which is common where a port, a free-trade zone or a finance centre sits between the origin and the final market. Each form carries its own documentation and its own exchange-control consequences.

blocks.caption: Forms of foreign trade
rows: Payment abroad, goods enter, foreign exchange outflow
Receipt from abroad, goods leave, foreign exchange inflow
In through one country and out to a third
Value added locally as commission or processing

blocks.text: The importance of foreign trade lies in what a country cannot do for itself. No single nation holds every raw material, every climate and every technology, so trade allows each country to specialise in what it produces at the lowest relative cost and to obtain the rest by exchange. For an economy, exports bring in foreign exchange needed to pay for essential imports, they widen the market beyond domestic demand so firms can achieve scale, and they expose domestic producers to competition that keeps quality and price honest.

items: Specialisation raises world output, because each country does what it does best.
Imports give access to materials, machinery and goods the country cannot make.
Exports earn the foreign exchange that pays for those imports.
Competition from abroad disciplines domestic pricing and quality.
Entrepot trade earns service income without requiring domestic raw materials.

learn.title: Balance of trade and balance of payments

blocks.text: The balance of trade is the difference between the value of a country’s visible exports and its visible imports over a period, so it records only merchandise. A deficit arises when imports of goods exceed exports, and a surplus when exports exceed imports. The balance of payments is a wider record: it covers not only visible trade but also invisible items such as shipping, insurance and tourism, plus capital flows such as borrowing, investment and transfers. The balance of payments must always balance in an accounting sense, because every payment has a corresponding receipt, whereas the balance of trade can and often does run a deficit.

blocks.caption: Balance of trade against balance of payments
rows: Visible and invisible items plus capital flows
Yes, surplus or deficit is normal
Must balance in the accounting sense

items.text: A country imports machinery worth more than it exports in goods.
items.note: The balance of trade shows a deficit even if its shipping and software services earn enough abroad to balance the wider account.

items.text: Remittances sent home by citizens working abroad.
items.note: A credit in the balance of payments, though it forms no part of the balance of trade.

blocks.text: Foreign trade runs on documents because the parties rarely meet and each institution needs its own proof. The transaction begins with a proforma invoice, which is the seller’s quotation stating the goods, price and terms before the order is confirmed. Once the goods move, the commercial invoice states the actual amount payable, and the packing list gives the contents, weights and dimensions of each package for customs and the buyer. The customs entry is filed to clear the consignment in or out of the country, and the certificate of origin states where the goods were made, which matters for preferential duty treatment.

blocks.caption: Principal foreign trade documents and their purpose
rows: Quotation before the order: goods, price, terms

Final amount payable for the consignment
Contents, weights and marks of each package
Receipt for goods and document of title for sea shipment
Receipt and contract for air carriage, not a document of title
Evidence that the consignment is covered in transit
Bank’s conditional undertaking to pay against documents

blocks.text: The bill of lading deserves particular attention because it does three jobs at once: it is a receipt from the shipping line for the goods received on board, it is evidence of the contract of carriage, and it is a document of title, which means whoever holds the original can claim the goods. An airway bill by contrast is only a receipt and contract, and the consignee named in it remains the owner, which is why air shipments are settled differently.

learn.title: The letter of credit and the risk problem it solves

blocks.text: The central problem of foreign trade is that neither party trusts the other. The exporter fears sending goods and not being paid by a buyer in another legal system; the importer fears paying and receiving goods of the wrong description. The letter of credit solves both problems at once by substituting a bank for the counterparty. The importer asks her bank to issue a letter of credit in favour of the exporter, and that bank undertakes to pay against the presentation of documents that comply strictly with the terms stated, the usual requirement being the invoice, the bill of lading and the insurance document.

blocks.caption: Sequence of a documentary letter of credit
rows: Exporter and importer agree the contract and the credit terms
Importer applies to her bank to open a credit in the exporter’s favour
Issuing bank informs the exporter through an advising bank
Exporter ships the goods and gathers the documents required
Documents presented to the bank and checked for strict compliance
Bank pays against conforming documents and debits the importer

items: The exporter gains a bank’s payment undertaking instead of a stranger’s promise.
The importer gains control over what is paid for, since payment follows documents describing the goods.
The bank earns a fee and pays only against documents, not against the goods themselves.
Discrepancies cause rejection, so accuracy in the documents is as important as the goods.

keyPoints: Foreign trade is trade between residents of different countries.
Its three forms are import, export and entrepot trade.
Trade lets each country specialise in what it produces at the lowest relative cost.
Exports earn the foreign exchange needed to pay for essential imports.
Balance of trade covers visible goods only and can run a deficit.
Balance of payments covers visible, invisible and capital items and must balance in the accounting sense.
Proforma invoice is the quotation; commercial invoice is the final amount payable.
Bill of lading is receipt, evidence of carriage and document of title.
Airway bill is a receipt and contract but not a document of title.
A letter of credit substitutes a bank’s undertaking for the counterparty’s promise.

questions.prompt: Bringing goods into a country for sale is:
questions.explanation: Import trade moves goods into the country and involves an outflow of foreign exchange to the seller.

questions.prompt: Goods imported into one country and re-exported to a third country without processing is:
questions.explanation: Entrepot trade uses a third country as a route or staging point, earning service income rather than adding material value.

questions.prompt: Which document is a document of title in sea transport?
questions.explanation: Holding the original bill of lading entitles the holder to claim the goods, whereas an airway bill names a consignee without transferring title.

questions.prompt: Under a letter of credit, the issuing bank pays:
options: As soon as the goods arrive at the port
Only against a set of documents that strictly compliles with the credit terms
Whenever the exporter asks for payment
After the importer inspects and approves the goods
questions.answer: Only against a set of documents that strictly compliles with the credit terms
questions.explanation: The bank’s undertaking is documentary: it examines papers, not goods, and pays only when they comply exactly with the terms.

questions.prompt: The wider record that covers visible trade, invisible services and capital flows is called the balance of __________ .
questions.explanation: The balance of payments is the complete statement of a country’s external transactions and must balance in the accounting sense, unlike the balance of trade which can show a deficit.

questions.prompt: The document issued by a bank undertaking to pay the exporter against a complying set of documents is a letter of __________ .
questions.explanation: The credit substitutes the bank’s credit standing for the exporter’s trust in a buyer in another country.

questions.prompt: State four reasons why foreign trade is important to a country.
questions.answer: Four reasons are: it allows each country to specialise in the goods it can produce at the lowest relative cost, raising world output; it gives access to raw materials, machinery and goods the country cannot produce itself; it earns the foreign exchange required to pay for essential imports; and it exposes domestic producers to competition, which keeps quality and prices honest. It also widens the market so firms can produce at scale.
questions.explanation: Each reason must explain the mechanism, since a bare assertion of importance earns only partial credit.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the balance of trade and the balance of payments.
questions.answer: The balance of trade records only visible merchandise exports against visible merchandise imports, so it can show a surplus or a deficit. The balance of payments is a wider record covering those visible items plus invisible services such as freight, insurance and tourism, income and transfers, and capital movements such as loans and investment, and it balances in the accounting sense because every payment has a matching receipt. A country can therefore run a trade deficit while its balance of payments is in equilibrium.
questions.explanation: Three points of scope are needed, together with the statement that only the trade balance can be unbalanced.

questions.prompt: List the documents used in foreign trade and explain the purpose of any five.
questions.answer: The principal documents are the proforma invoice, commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading, airway bill, customs entry, certificate of origin, insurance certificate and letter of credit. The proforma invoice is the quotation issued before the order, stating goods, price and terms, and it is what the importer uses to apply for a letter of credit. The commercial invoice states the final amount payable for the consignment and is the basis of customs valuation. The packing list gives the contents, weights and marks of each package so that customs and the buyer can check the consignment without opening every case. The bill of lading performs three functions: it is the shipping line’s receipt for the goods, evidence of the contract of carriage, and a document of title that allows the holder to claim the consignment. The certificate of origin states where the goods were manufactured, which determines the duty rate applied. The letter of credit is the bank’s conditional undertaking to pay against a complying document set.
questions.explanation: Full marks require five documents each with a distinct purpose, and the three-part role of the bill of lading should be stated explicitly.

questions.prompt: An exporter has shipped goods but the bill of lading shows a weight that differs from the packing list, and the bank has refused to pay under the letter of credit. Explain what has happened and what the exporter should do.
questions.answer: The bank has examined only the documents and found that they do not agree with each other, so they do not strictly comply with the terms of the credit. Under a documentary credit the bank is bound to pay against conforming documents and has no authority to accept goods or to overlook a discrepancy, so the weight difference, however small, is a valid ground for refusal even though the goods themselves may be perfectly in order. What has happened is therefore a documentary failure rather than a commercial dispute. The exporter should obtain a corrected document from the shipping line or issue a corrected packing list so that the set is consistent, re-present it within the validity of the credit, and in parallel ask the buyer to accept the discrepancy by an amendment or a waiver so that payment does not wait for the paperwork. To prevent a recurrence, the exporter should check that the invoice, packing list, bill of lading and letter of credit all state identical weights, quantities and descriptions before presentation, since banks pay for consistency on paper, not for the condition of the cargo.
questions.explanation: The answer earns marks for identifying documentary non-compliance as the cause, explaining why the bank may not inspect the goods, and giving both the immediate remedy and the preventive control.
